stops.name: Heidelberg, the Judengasse of the Electoral Palatinate
stops.campa: In the Jewish quarter of Heidelberg, in the ruined Palatinate lately burned by the armies of Louis XIV, a son is born to Issachar Süßkind Oppenheimer, a cantor and leader of a wandering troupe of players and singers, and to Michele, daughter of Salomon the reader of Frankfurt. They name him Joseph Süß, the sweet one. He carries in his blood the great Oppenheimer name, that clan of court-factors who lend to emperors. The father will die young. The boy is left to an uncle, to trade, and to the roads of the German courts.

stops.name: Vienna: the shadow of Samuel Oppenheimer, the Fugger of his day
stops.campa: In Vienna dies Samuel Oppenheimer, kinsman of the clan, the great war-factor who armed the Empire against the Turk and lent to the House of Habsburg until it could not repay him: Prince Eugene's paymaster, called the Fugger of his age. His house is stormed, his fortune denied, his memory blackened. The Court Jew's tragedy is written a generation before Joseph Süß walks into it: raise a prince, arm a state, and be devoured when the prince has done with you. The thread runs from Vienna to Stuttgart, and Joseph will follow it to its end.

stops.name: Amsterdam, the merchant houses and the diamond trade
stops.campa: The young man travels through Amsterdam, Vienna, Prague, learning the arts of the wandering factor: bills of exchange, the price of jewels, the ways of lending to men who outrank him and hate to be indebted. In Amsterdam he sees the great Sephardic houses and the diamond bourse, the machinery of a credit that circles Europe. He acquires manners, French, an ease among aristocrats, and the taste for fine linen and finer women that the chronicles will one day fling in his face. He is charming, quick, and utterly without protection but his wits.

stops.name: Prague, the old city of the factors
stops.campa: In Prague, the great capital of Ashkenaz, he moves among the largest Jewish community of the Empire: the crooked lanes of Josefov, the merchant families, the court-factors who supply the Habsburg war-machine. Here the network of the Oppenheimers reaches its densest weave: cousins, credit, correspondents in every princely seat. He learns that a Jew may sit at a duke's right hand and remain, in law, a thing to be tolerated, taxed, and expelled at will. He carries that knowledge lightly, as a young man does, and rides west toward the Rhine.

stops.name: Mannheim, factor to the Palatine court
stops.campa: At Mannheim he sets up as a private financier, serving the Elector Palatine and the Elector of Cologne. The trade is money and its shadows: loans, jewels, army supply, the quiet brokering of offices. He is good at it: better than good. The courts of the little German states are hungry for credit and short of scruple, and a factor who can conjure gold where the treasury is dry is worth his weight in privileges. Mannheim is the first stone of a rising he will not be able to stop when it turns to a fall.

stops.name: Darmstadt, the Hessian purse
stops.campa: He works the court of Hesse-Darmstadt, one more princely seat added to his circuit of the Rhineland. The pattern is fixed now: a Jew of no standing who nonetheless dines with landgraves, arranges their debts, and takes his commission in coin and in the toleration that lets him live outside the ghetto walls. He is building the reputation that will carry him to Württemberg: a man who makes money appear. Behind him already trail the resentments of officials he has outpaced and creditors he has outmaneuvered.

stops.name: Frankfurt am Main, the Golden Swan outside the Judengasse
stops.campa: Frankfurt becomes his base. His mother lives in the Judengasse, that narrow, locked and crowded lane; but Joseph Süß, by his rank and his usefulness, is suffered to lodge outside its gates at the Golden Swan inn, and keeps a comfortable house of his own. It is a scandal and a privilege both: a Jew sleeping beyond the ghetto wall. Here he trades, lends, brokers, and waits. Frankfurt is the crossroads of the German money-world, and it is here, soon, that a discontented prince will find the man who will make him rich.

stops.name: Bad Wildbad, the spa where he meets Karl Alexander
stops.campa: In the Black Forest spa of Wildbad, taking the waters, Joseph Süß is introduced to Karl Alexander, Prince of Württemberg: a Catholic convert, an imperial general, a soldier chronically short of money and long on ambition. Something clicks between them: the prince who needs gold, the factor who conjures it. Here begins the fatal partnership. Karl Alexander sees a purse; Joseph Süß sees a throne to serve and a fortune to make. Neither reads the ending already written in the fate of Samuel Oppenheimer at Vienna.

stops.name: Frankfurt, appointed Hoffaktor and keeper of the privy purse
stops.campa: In November the prince names him Hoffaktor and Schatullenverwalter: court-factor and administrator of the privy purse. Joseph Süß now handles Karl Alexander's private money, his debts, his ambitions. He knows how to please: 'I knew how to accommodate the lord's temperament,' he will say. He supplies jewels for the prince's wife, gold for his schemes, and the loans that make a debtor prince into a grateful one. The rise is dizzying. He does not yet live at Stuttgart, but Stuttgart is already his destination.
stops.quote: Ich habe mich in des Herrn Humor zu schicken gewußt.

stops.name: Stuttgart, the accession of Karl Alexander as Duke
stops.campa: Eberhard Ludwig dies and Karl Alexander becomes Duke of Württemberg: a Catholic ruler over a fiercely Protestant land, ringed by suspicious Estates who guard the old constitution. He brings his factor with him. Joseph Süß rises to real power: minister-resident at Frankfurt, commissary of the Swabian army, and soon the hand behind the whole ducal finance. A Jew now stands at the center of a Lutheran duchy's treasury. The Estates watch, and hate, and begin to keep their accounts of grievance against the day the duke should die.

stops.name: Stuttgart, the Mint reformed and the coinage debased
stops.campa: He takes the ducal Mint in hand. New coin flows: lighter, baser, its silver quietly thinned, its face value held. The treasury fills; the people's purses empty as the debased Landmünze buys less bread each month. To the court it is genius: money made from nothing. To the burghers and the pastors it is theft dressed as reform, and the Jew's name is stamped on every clipped coin. The Mint becomes the first article of the indictment being written against him in the hearts of the estates.

stops.name: Stuttgart, the monopolies: salt, tobacco, leather, wine
stops.campa: He seizes the trades for the crown: salt, tobacco, leather, wine; the free commerce of the towns turned into ducal monopolies that pour their profit into Karl Alexander's coffers and Joseph Süß's commission. He founds manufactories of silk and porcelain, and the first bank of southern Germany, building an absolutist economy on the French model. It is modern, ruthless, and to the guilds and Estates an intolerable robbery. Every merchant squeezed, every office sold through his Gratialamt, becomes an enemy who will testify against him when the wheel turns.
